title: The Oyster Helpers of Chesapeake Bay
summary:
John Consoli lives on Kent Island in Maryland. From his pier, he pulls up a mesh bag full of oysters from Chesapeake Bay. In just three months, he says, they have grown so much that the bag is hard to lift.

Oysters do a lot of good. Each adult oyster cleans up to 50 gallons of water a day. Cleaner water helps sea grass grow, and sea grass helps crabs. Oyster shells also give small fish and crabs places to live and hide.

Long ago, the bay had huge numbers of oysters. But people took too many, and by 2011 their numbers had fallen by over 99%, according to one estimate. Now oyster farming is growing, and wild oysters are coming back a little, biologist Ryan Carnegie says.

Consoli asks his neighbours to help through his Peer to Pier Network. His wife, Kathy, says he may have reached 80 people. Robots may help too. A robot called Oysterbot maps the seabed, so farmers know where to plant oysters.
why_it_matters: It shows children that helping one small animal, like an oyster, can also help clean water and many other animals.

background_read: Oysters are sea animals with hard shells that live in the water and clean it as they feed.
Chesapeake Bay once had huge numbers of oysters, but people took too many and their numbers fell greatly.
Now people grow oysters and help wild ones return, which also helps sea grass, crabs and small fish.
Article_Structure: WHO: John Consoli, his wife Kathy, his neighbours, and biologist Ryan Carnegie.
WHAT: Consoli grows oysters in a mesh bag and asks neighbours to help through his Peer to Pier Network.
WHERE: On Kent Island in Maryland, in the waters of Chesapeake Bay.
WHY: Oysters clean the water, help sea grass grow and give small fish and crabs places to live, after their numbers fell when people took too many.
